prompt: A fintech's Java and Python services pull open source libraries from public registries. The security review wants libraries that Google builds from source in a hardened pipeline, with signed SLSA provenance and SBOMs, and patched as vulnerabilities appear. What fits best?

choices.text: Create Artifact Registry remote repositories for PyPI and Maven Central so packages are cached next to the build runners.
choices.rationale: Remote repositories cache and proxy upstream content; they do not vouch for how the packages were built or sign them.

choices.text: Rely on Artifact Analysis scanning to flag known CVEs in whichever libraries developers choose to pull from public sources.
choices.rationale: Scanning reports known vulnerabilities but does not rebuild packages in a trusted pipeline or provide provenance for them.

choices.text: Consume curated packages from Assured Open Source Software, which Google builds securely and serves via Artifact Registry.
choices.rationale: Correct: Assured OSS packages carry SLSA level 3 provenance and SBOMs, and Google scans and fixes vulnerabilities in the curated set.

choices.text: Require Binary Authorization attestations from the build pipeline for every library the services import at runtime.
choices.rationale: Binary Authorization gates container image deployment; it does not source or attest individual third-party library packages.

explanation: Assured OSS is the supplier-side control: verified builds, tamper-evident provenance, SPDX SBOMs and VEX data. It is delivered through Artifact Registry repositories (the free tier covers Python, Go and Java).

prompt: Internal Python package payments-core lives in a private Artifact Registry repository. A build just installed an identically named package with a higher version from the public index, through a remote repository proxying PyPI. The team uses a virtual repository for pip. Which change best prevents this class of attack?

choices.text: Publish the internal package with a very large version number so it always wins pip version resolution.
choices.rationale: This is a brittle workaround that depends on every release outranking anything an attacker publishes; it is not a control.

choices.text: Raise the priority of the PyPI remote repository in the virtual repository so public versions are evaluated first.
choices.rationale: This is the opposite of the fix: ranking the public upstream first is what makes dependency confusion possible.

choices.text: Rank the private repository above the PyPI remote repository in the virtual repository's upstream priorities.
choices.rationale: Correct: a virtual repository can prioritize private repositories over remote ones, so internal names resolve privately first.

choices.text: Enable automatic vulnerability scanning on the private repository so malicious public packages are caught at install.
choices.rationale: Scanning looks for known vulnerabilities in stored artifacts; it does not change which repository serves a package name.

explanation: Dependency confusion exploits search order across public and private sources. Upstream priority in a virtual repository is the documented mitigation.

prompt: Cymbal Retail's product teams each build gen AI agents in their own projects. The central security team wants a baseline screening Gemini calls across the organization without each team opting in. It also wants any template a team creates to be no less strict than the floor settings in effect, and wants only the security team to be able to change those floor settings. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Publish a recommended Model Armor template and ask each team to reference it in its calls, with a quarterly review of how teams comply.
choices.rationale: A published template is voluntary; any team that forgets to reference it sends unscreened prompts and nothing blocks weaker templates.

choices.text: Place a Cloud Armor WAF policy in front of each agent's web frontend with the OWASP rule set enabled for every project that hosts an agent.
choices.rationale: A WAF inspects HTTP traffic patterns; it does not evaluate prompts and responses for injection, jailbreaks or leaked data.

choices.text: Give each project owner full control of Model Armor settings so that thresholds match each team's false-positive rate and release schedule.
choices.rationale: Settings lower in the resource hierarchy take precedence, so letting every project owner edit floor settings gives no common baseline, and a team could loosen or disable it.

choices.text: Set organization-level floor settings with enforcement enabled, and grant the Floor Setting Admin role only to the security team.
choices.rationale: Floor settings set at the organization apply to everything within it, and Model Armor will not create or update a template that is less strict than the floor settings. Because settings lower in the hierarchy take precedence, restricting who holds the floor-settings admin role is what keeps the baseline from being loosened.

explanation: Floor settings can be set at organization, folder or project level; settings lower in the hierarchy take precedence, and enforcement of template conformance is controlled by a flag that defaults to false. Pair floor settings with IAM limits on who may change them.

prompt: Which statements about how Model Armor works are correct? Choose three.

choices.text: The application or gateway calls the sanitize methods for prompts and responses; Model Armor does not invoke the LLM itself.
choices.rationale: Correct: it is a screening layer; both sanitizeUserPrompt and sanitizeModelResponse are optional calls your pipeline makes.

choices.text: It durably stores every analyzed prompt and response by default so security teams can replay incidents later.
choices.rationale: Model Armor is stateless and discards content after analysis; data persists only if Cloud Logging is explicitly enabled.

choices.text: Its advanced Sensitive Data Protection configuration can de-identify detected data, while the basic configuration only inspects.
choices.rationale: Correct: advanced mode uses SDP templates to transform, tokenize or redact; basic mode is limited to detection.

choices.text: It can screen only Gemini models that run in the same Google Cloud project as the template and nothing else.
choices.rationale: Its API-based design lets it screen prompts and responses for models in other clouds or projects too.

choices.text: Inspect-only mode records findings without blocking, so Cloud Logging must be enabled to get any value from it.
choices.rationale: Correct: inspect only logs matches and lets the request proceed, so without Cloud Logging the findings are never visible.

explanation: Model Armor is a stateless, cloud-agnostic screening service. Blocking requires inspect-and-block enforcement; inspect-only is for tuning.

prompt: A support chatbot's Model Armor template uses inspect-only enforcement and the Low-and-above confidence level for the prompt-injection filter. Cloud Logging shows hundreds of MATCH_FOUND results per day, yet the model answered every one of those prompts. The team wants real blocking without blocking many legitimate users. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Keep inspect-only and add a system prompt telling the model to ignore any instructions found inside user input.
choices.rationale: A system prompt is a soft instruction the attacker is already trying to override; it does not stop the request from reaching the model.

choices.text: Switch to inspect-and-block but keep Low-and-above, since stopping every weak signal is the safest setting for a customer-facing bot.
choices.rationale: Low-and-above flags any indication of an attack; blocking at that level maximizes false positives for legitimate users.

choices.text: Move to inspect-and-block, raise confidence to Medium-and-above, and review the logged matches to check block quality.
choices.rationale: Correct: blocking needs inspect-and-block, and starting at High or Medium-and-above is the documented way to limit false positives.

choices.text: Delete the template, because matches that did not stop the model show the filter cannot detect injections here.
choices.rationale: The logged matches show the filter is detecting; the answers were delivered because the enforcement mode never blocks.

explanation: MATCH_FOUND with a delivered answer is the signature of inspect-only mode. Tune confidence using the logs, then enforce.

prompt: A health-insurance analytics team shares claims extracts with a data science group. Member IDs are 12-digit numbers, the downstream schema rejects anything that is not 12 digits, the same member must map to the same value in every table, and the privacy office must be able to re-identify a member for lawful requests. Which Sensitive Data Protection transformation fits?

choices.text: Deterministic encryption with AES-SIV, which is reversible and consistent but outputs base64 text.
choices.rationale: Reversible and consistent, but the base64 output does not preserve length or character set, so the 12-digit schema would reject it.

choices.text: Cryptographic hashing with HMAC-SHA-256, which gives consistent tokens that cannot be reversed.
choices.rationale: Consistent tokens help joins, but hashing cannot be reversed, so the privacy office could never re-identify a member.

choices.text: Character masking that replaces all but the last four digits with a masking symbol.
choices.rationale: Masking is irreversible and collapses many members onto the same value, which breaks both joins and re-identification.

choices.text: Format-preserving encryption (FFX) with a KMS-wrapped key, keeping length and digits and staying reversible.
choices.rationale: Correct: FPE-FFX preserves length and character set, supports surrogates, is reversible, and gives equal tokens for equal inputs under one key.

explanation: Compare the three pseudonymization methods on reversibility and format: AES-SIV (reversible, not format-preserving), FPE-FFX (reversible, format-preserving), HMAC-SHA-256 (not reversible).

prompt: A company suspects sensitive data is scattered across hundreds of BigQuery datasets, Cloud SQL databases and Cloud Storage buckets in many projects. It wants an ongoing inventory of where that data lives and how risky it is, without writing scan jobs per resource. What should it use?

choices.text: Cloud Asset Inventory exports searched for column names such as ssn or email across all projects.
choices.rationale: Names are a weak proxy: sensitive values hide in columns with innocuous names, and the export says nothing about content.

choices.text: Sensitive Data Protection discovery with an organization-level scan configuration that generates data profiles.
choices.rationale: Correct: discovery profiles supported sources automatically, scores sensitivity and risk, and can publish to Security Command Center and Dataplex.

choices.text: Cloud Audit Logs Data Access entries queried for reads of any column that might contain personal data, across all projects.
choices.rationale: Audit logs record who accessed data, not what the data contains, and they cannot reveal never-accessed sensitive columns.

choices.text: A VPC Service Controls dry-run perimeter report that lists every resource holding regulated data.
choices.rationale: Dry-run reports show which API calls would violate a perimeter; they do not classify the contents of resources.

explanation: Discovery configurations can be set at organization, folder or project level, and default to reprofiling every 30 days when data changes.

prompt: EHR Healthcare's engineering VP says that because Google Cloud supports HIPAA, EHR can move patient workloads without further compliance work on its own side. What is the most accurate response?

choices.text: Google offers a BAA and secures the infrastructure, but EHR must still configure its environment and applications correctly.
choices.rationale: Correct: HIPAA compliance is a shared responsibility; customers remain responsible for how their environment and applications are configured.

choices.text: Workloads with PHI must run in a dedicated region that Google certifies specifically for health data.
choices.rationale: The BAA covers Google Cloud's entire infrastructure across regions and zones; no special health region is required.

choices.text: Signing the BAA transfers HIPAA liability for the stored data to Google, so EHR's duties end there.
choices.rationale: The BAA defines Google's obligations as a business associate; it does not move the customer's responsibility for its own setup.

choices.text: Services under the BAA arrive preconfigured with least-privilege access and full audit logging for PHI.
choices.rationale: Access controls and Data Access audit logging must be configured by the customer; defaults do not provide this.

explanation: Coverage under the BAA does not equal a compliant deployment. Customer-side controls such as IAM, encryption choices and logging hygiene remain EHR's job.

prompt: EHR Healthcare's platform team reviews how patient data could leak through operational metadata in its GKE and logging stack. Which practices fit Google's HIPAA guidance? Choose two.

choices.text: Use opaque identifiers in labels, resource names and log fields instead of patient names or record numbers.
choices.rationale: Correct: Google's HIPAA guidance says to avoid PHI in resource metadata and logs, so identifiers must not reveal the patient.

choices.text: Name Pub/Sub topics after the patient so on-call engineers can trace a message to a person quickly.
choices.rationale: Topic names are resource metadata visible to many principals; putting patient names there exposes PHI outside the protected data path.

choices.text: Restrict who can read application logs and export audit logs to a controlled, access-restricted destination.
choices.rationale: Correct: strict IAM on logs and exporting audit logs to a protected location are part of the recommended practices.

choices.text: Add the patient's details to Cloud Monitoring alert documentation so responders have full context in notifications.
choices.rationale: Alert configuration is monitoring metadata and must never carry PHI; notifications fan out to email and chat tools.

choices.text: Turn off default logging on every covered service so that no log entry can ever contain PHI.
choices.rationale: Disabling logging removes audit evidence the regulation expects; the fix is to keep PHI out of logs, not logs out of the system.

explanation: PHI belongs in the protected data stores. Names, labels, log lines and alert text are operational metadata that many people can read.

prompt: Auditors ask EU-based Nordhaven Pay to evidence that customer data is stored only in the EU. The team sets gcp.resourceLocations to allow in:eu-locations at the organization node, but 300 buckets and datasets were already created in US regions last year. What does the constraint do about those?

choices.text: Nothing: it governs only where newly created resources can be placed, so existing US resources must be migrated.
choices.rationale: Correct: after you define resource locations the limitation applies only to newly created resources; existing ones are untouched.

choices.text: It blocks reads of the existing US data by EU principals until the resources are moved into allowed locations by an admin.
choices.rationale: The constraint restricts resource creation locations; it never evaluates who reads existing data.

choices.text: It relocates each existing resource to the nearest allowed EU location in the background over several days.
choices.rationale: No relocation happens; moving data is a manual migration or recreation task.

choices.text: It marks the existing resources noncompliant and makes them read-only until an exception is approved.
choices.rationale: Org policy has no such state transition for existing resources; they remain fully writable.

explanation: Resource-location policy is a preventive guardrail for creation. It also does not cover global resources or services that cannot choose a location, so evidence needs migration plus inventory checks.

prompt: Brightwave Labs wants to enforce constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices for BigQuery and Cloud Storage across 400 projects but fears breaking pipelines, so it creates the policy in dry-run mode. After a week the org policy audit logs show 38 entries with dryRunResult DENIED and liveResult ALLOWED, all from two projects. What does this mean and what should happen next?

choices.text: Those resources were created without CMEK and will be re-encrypted automatically at enforcement, so no action is needed.
choices.rationale: Enforcement affects only newly created resources; nothing is re-encrypted retroactively, and the dry-run entries are warnings.

choices.text: Those 38 operations were already blocked in production, so the two teams must request approval to continue.
choices.rationale: LiveResult ALLOWED shows the operations went through; dry run never blocks anything.

choices.text: The ALLOWED live result means the policy is misconfigured and should be deleted and recreated before testing again.
choices.rationale: The DENIED-versus-ALLOWED pair is the intended output of dry run, showing what enforcement would change.

choices.text: Those 38 creations would be denied once enforced; have the teams adopt CMEK or get an exception, then enforce.
choices.rationale: Correct: dryRunResult DENIED with liveResult ALLOWED identifies operations enforcement would block, so fix or exempt them first.

explanation: Dry-run policies audit-log violations without denying them. Query for dryRunResult DENIED and liveResult ALLOWED to find the callers an enforcement switch would break.

prompt: A healthcare SaaS wants guardrails so new BigQuery datasets, Cloud Storage buckets and Cloud SQL instances across the organization must use CMEK, with keys coming only from a central security-owned KMS project. Which statements describe the right use of organization policies? Choose two.

choices.text: List those services in constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices so creating a resource without a Cloud KMS key fails.
choices.rationale: Correct: with the constraint active, create requests for the listed services do not succeed without a Cloud KMS key.

choices.text: Enforcing either constraint re-encrypts existing resources with a key from the allowed KMS project.
choices.rationale: CMEK organization policies apply only to newly created resources; existing resources are unaffected.

choices.text: Set constraints/gcp.restrictCmekCryptoKeyProjects to allow only the central KMS project as the key source.
choices.rationale: Correct: this constraint limits which projects, folders or organizations CMEK keys may come from.

choices.text: The constraints cover every Google Cloud service, so no per-service support check is required.
choices.rationale: They cover a large but finite list of supported services (50 or more); unsupported services need a check.

choices.text: Apply the constraint separately in every project, since new projects cannot inherit organization-level policies.
choices.rationale: Organization policies inherit down the hierarchy to new projects, which is why setting them at the org or folder works.

explanation: Two constraints, two jobs: one requires CMEK, one restricts where keys come from. Neither fixes resources that already exist.

prompt: After a records export was copied out of a Cloud Storage bucket, EHR Healthcare's investigators find Admin Activity logs for bucket configuration changes but no record of which identities read the objects. What explains this and what is the fix?

choices.text: Cloud Storage never emits object-read audit records; only VPC Flow Logs can show who read an object.
choices.rationale: Cloud Storage supports DATA_READ audit logs once enabled; flow logs show network flows, not object-level identities.

choices.text: Admin Activity logs rotate after 30 days in the default bucket, so the earlier object reads were deleted before anyone looked.
choices.rationale: Admin Activity logs sit in the _Required bucket for 400 days, and they never contain data reads in the first place.

choices.text: Data Access logs are off by default for Cloud Storage; enable DATA_READ in the audit config at org or folder level.
choices.rationale: Correct: Data Access audit logs are disabled by default (except for some BigQuery logs) and are enabled through auditConfigs in IAM policy.

choices.text: Object-read audit entries appear only after Access Transparency is enabled for the project that owns the bucket.
choices.rationale: Access Transparency logs Google personnel access; it has no effect on whether customer reads are audit logged.

explanation: Admin Activity logs are always on. Reads of user data are Data Access logs, which you enable (and pay for) deliberately.

prompt: Auditors need DATA_READ records for every principal in the clinical-analytics project, but entries for etl-runner are missing. A project-level audit config without any exemption was already applied. Based on the exhibit, which explanation and action are correct?

exhibit.label: IAM audit configs (excerpts)
exhibit.content:
# organizations/412345 IAM policy
auditConfigs:
- service: allServices
  auditLogConfigs:
  - logType: DATA_READ
    exemptedMembers:
    - serviceAccount:etl-runner@data-platform.iam.gserviceaccount.com
  - logType: DATA_WRITE

# projects/clinical-analytics IAM policy
auditConfigs:
- service: allServices
  auditLogConfigs:
  - logType: DATA_READ
  - logType: DATA_WRITE

choices.text: The project-level config replaces the org config, so etl-runner is audited and it simply never read any data.
choices.rationale: Project settings cannot override or replace a parent's audit configuration; the two combine, and the exemption survives.

choices.text: Service accounts are always excluded from Data Access audit logs regardless of any configuration applied.
choices.rationale: Data Access logs do record service account activity unless that principal is exempted; there is no blanket exclusion.

choices.text: The org-level exemption is inherited and exemptions accumulate, so remove it at the org or accept the exemption.
choices.rationale: Correct: project-level settings cannot disable inherited configuration or remove inherited exempted principals, so the fix is at the org.

choices.text: allServices excludes BigQuery, so add a separate bigquery.googleapis.com entry at project level to log the reads.
choices.rationale: allServices covers every service that supports Data Access logs; adding a service entry would not remove the exemption.

explanation: Audit configs combine as a union up the hierarchy. A lower level can add logging, but cannot subtract an inherited exemption.

prompt: A telehealth company's policy requires audit logs to be kept for seven years and protected from deletion or shortened retention, even by project owners. Which steps meet this? Choose two.

choices.text: Route audit logs with an organization-level aggregated sink into a log bucket in a dedicated security project.
choices.rationale: Correct: centralizing logs in a separate, tightly controlled project keeps them out of reach of individual project owners.

choices.text: Raise the _Required bucket retention to seven years in every project so the default storage already complies.
choices.rationale: The _Required bucket's 400-day retention is fixed and cannot be changed, so it cannot meet a seven-year rule.

choices.text: Keep logs in each project's _Default bucket and raise its retention, relying on owners not to change it.
choices.rationale: Project owners can still edit or delete that bucket's settings, so the protection requirement is not met.

choices.text: Set the destination bucket's retention to about 2,555 days and lock it so it cannot be shortened or deleted early.
choices.rationale: Correct: custom buckets allow retention up to 3,650 days, and locking is irreversible, which prevents reduction or early deletion.

choices.text: Add a sink exclusion so that only Admin Activity entries are kept and Data Access entries are dropped to save cost.
choices.rationale: Dropping Data Access entries removes read evidence the policy needs, and it does nothing about immutability.

explanation: Centralize in a restricted project, set the custom bucket retention, and lock it. Remember that locking is irreversible, so size the retention deliberately.

prompt: A broker-dealer must keep trade confirmations unmodifiable and undeletable for six years in Cloud Storage. The compliance lead worries that locking the retention policy could prevent correcting a mistaken setting later. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: A project owner can remove a locked retention policy after confirming the bucket name in the console.
choices.rationale: Once locked, the policy cannot be removed by anyone, owners included; that is what makes it usable as immutable storage.

choices.text: A locked policy can be lengthened but not removed or shortened, so set the period deliberately before locking.
choices.rationale: Correct: after locking you may increase the retention period, but you cannot remove or reduce it, and locking is irreversible.

choices.text: Locking applies only to new uploads, so objects already in the bucket remain deletable until they are overwritten.
choices.rationale: A retention policy applies retroactively to existing objects as well as to new uploads.

choices.text: Locking can be undone within 30 days by Cloud Support, after which the retention period becomes permanent.
choices.rationale: There is no grace window; locking is irreversible and support cannot reverse it.

explanation: Bucket Lock supports WORM-style regulatory retention. Locking also adds a project lien that blocks project deletion until the lien is removed.

prompt: A European bank wants Google support and engineering staff to access its content only with its explicit consent. Which statements about Access Approval are correct? Choose two.

choices.text: Access Transparency must first be enabled for the organization before Access Approval can be turned on.
choices.rationale: Correct: enabling Access Transparency for the organization is a prerequisite for Access Approval.

choices.text: Access Approval blocks all Google access to content, including access excluded from Access Transparency.
choices.rationale: Access Transparency exclusions also apply to Access Approval, so it is not a total block on every Google access.

choices.text: Google may auto-approve requests for time-sensitive outages, but this is disabled for EU Data Boundary deployments.
choices.rationale: Correct: auto-approval for time-sensitive outages exists, but is disabled for EU Data Boundary and Sovereign Controls deployments.

choices.text: Access Approval records actions of the bank's own administrators, replacing Admin Activity audit log entries.
choices.rationale: Customer admin actions are recorded by Cloud Audit Logs; Access Approval concerns Google personnel requests.

choices.text: Google reviewers grant their own requests and the bank is notified afterwards through an email report.
choices.rationale: The model is the reverse: customer administrators approve or deny each request before access is granted.

explanation: Access Transparency shows what Google staff did; Access Approval adds a customer consent gate before they do it, with documented exclusions and auto-approval rules.

prompt: MedLedger, a US healthcare analytics firm, wants every new project that processes PHI to inherit US-only data residency and CMEK support, plus visibility when configuration drifts from those guardrails. What should it do?

choices.text: Apply gcp.resourceLocations to each PHI project one by one and review the audit logs weekly for drift.
choices.rationale: This is manual per-project work with no package of related controls and no built-in violation monitoring.

choices.text: Enable Access Approval on the organization, which also constrains resource locations to the United States.
choices.rationale: Access Approval gates Google personnel access; it does not restrict where resources are created.

choices.text: Sign the Google Cloud BAA and rely on it to restrict where covered services can place data.
choices.rationale: A BAA is a contractual agreement, not a technical control; it does not enforce data placement.

choices.text: Create an Assured Workloads folder with a US healthcare control package and place the PHI projects inside it.
choices.rationale: Correct: the US Data Boundary for Healthcare and Life Sciences package enforces US-only regions, supports CMEK, and monitors for violations.

explanation: Assured Workloads applies control packages (org policy constraints and more) to a folder, so projects inside inherit guardrails and violation monitoring.

prompt: An EU insurer restricted resource locations with an organization policy. A review finds every project's _Default and _Required log buckets are in the global location, and auditors say the logs hold personal data that must stay in the EU. Which actions address this? Choose two.

choices.text: Set the organization's Cloud Logging default storage location to an EU region for newly created projects.
choices.rationale: Correct: default resource settings can set the storage location for new _Default and _Required buckets, though only for newly created resources.

choices.text: Update each existing project's _Default bucket to move it to an EU region in place.
choices.rationale: A bucket's location cannot be changed after creation; this operation does not exist.

choices.text: Apply the in:eu-locations constraint, which moves existing global log buckets into EU locations.
choices.rationale: Resource-location policy affects only new resources and never relocates existing ones.

choices.text: Create EU log buckets in existing projects and redirect the _Default sink so new entries are stored there.
choices.rationale: Correct: for existing projects the documented method is a user-defined regional bucket plus a redirected _Default sink.

choices.text: Disable the _Default sink in every project, since entries that are not stored cannot breach residency.
choices.rationale: Dropping logs removes operational and audit evidence, and other sinks and analysis services may still copy data.

explanation: Log buckets default to global and cannot be moved. Use org default settings for future projects and regional buckets with sink redirection for existing ones.

prompt: A retailer's BigQuery customer table has an email column. Support analysts should see masked emails while still querying the column with unchanged SQL, and the privacy team must see the raw values. What is the cleanest control?

choices.text: Add a row-level access policy so analysts only see rows whose email value is null, which hides most customers from them entirely.
choices.rationale: Row-level policies filter rows rather than values, and this would hide most customers instead of masking their emails.

choices.text: Hash the column in place with SHA-256 for every user so that nobody can read raw emails again.
choices.rationale: In-place hashing is destructive and removes the raw values the privacy team still needs.

choices.text: Create an authorized view without the email column and have analysts query that view instead.
choices.rationale: This forces analysts to change their SQL and removes the column rather than masking it for them.

choices.text: Tag the column with a policy tag, add an email-mask data policy, and grant Masked Reader and Fine-Grained Reader.
choices.rationale: Correct: masking builds on column-level access control; Masked Reader sees masked values while Fine-Grained Reader sees the originals.

explanation: BigQuery dynamic data masking needs a taxonomy, policy tags, data policies with masking rules, and role grants. Analysts keep their queries unchanged.

prompt: A customer's auditor asks a startup for evidence of the controls Google operates beneath its application, specifically Google Cloud's SOC 2 Type II report. Where can the startup obtain it directly?

choices.text: Security Command Center, which generates Google's attestation reports for each customer project on request in the console.
choices.rationale: Security Command Center reports on the customer's own configuration, not on Google's attestations.

choices.text: Compliance Reports Manager, Google's self-service portal for downloading compliance reports and certifications.
choices.rationale: Correct: Compliance Reports Manager is the self-service source for Google Cloud's SOC 2 and similar attestation reports.

choices.text: Cloud Audit Logs, where Google publishes its attestation as a periodic system event for each organization.
choices.rationale: Audit logs record API activity; they do not carry Google's third-party attestation reports.

choices.text: Assured Workloads, which issues a separate SOC 2 report for each workload folder that it creates.
choices.rationale: Assured Workloads applies control packages to a folder; it does not issue SOC 2 reports for customers.

explanation: Google's report covers Google's infrastructure controls. The startup still needs its own controls and, for its customers, its own SOC 2 for the application layer.

prompt: A CISO wants continuous, organization-wide evidence of how Google Cloud configurations measure against standards such as CIS and PCI DSS, with pass rates over time rather than a point-in-time audit. Which capability provides this?

choices.text: Organization Policy dry-run mode, which logs how each framework control would evaluate for every resource in the hierarchy.
choices.rationale: Dry run previews the effect of a constraint on API calls; it does not map configurations to framework controls.

choices.text: Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity, which scores each administrative change against the chosen standard.
choices.rationale: Audit logs record administrative actions and do not score configurations against standards.

choices.text: Security Command Center compliance monitoring, which maps detector findings to controls and reports pass rates.
choices.rationale: Correct: Security Command Center maps findings to framework controls and reports pass rates at org, folder or project level. Compliance Manager is the current mechanism; the legacy Security Health Analytics-based daily reports apply only when Compliance Manager is disabled.

choices.text: Assured Workloads folder creation, which certifies every project in the folder against a framework once.
choices.rationale: Assured Workloads sets guardrails for its control package and monitors them; it is not an org-wide framework pass-rate report.

explanation: Compliance monitoring is detective: it reports findings and pass rates, and remediation remains manual.

prompt: Altostrat Media is launching a customer-facing support chatbot on a Gemini model behind a Cloud Run service. Red-team testing shows that users can type instructions such as "ignore your previous rules" to manipulate the bot, and that it occasionally returns hateful language. The security team wants one centrally managed control that screens both prompts and responses and does not depend on the underlying model. What should the architect choose?

choices.text: Model Armor, with a template enabling prompt injection and jailbreak detection and responsible AI filters on prompts and responses
choices.rationale: Model Armor screens LLM prompts and responses, is model-agnostic, and offers prompt injection and jailbreak detection plus responsible AI filters such as hate speech, managed through templates and floor settings.

choices.text: Cloud Armor in front of the service, with preconfigured WAF rules enabled to block malicious request patterns before the app
choices.rationale: Cloud Armor WAF rules target web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, not manipulation of an LLM through natural-language text, and it does not screen what the model returns.

choices.text: Sensitive Data Protection inspection on every prompt and response, redacting any findings before text reaches the model or user
choices.rationale: Sensitive Data Protection discovers and de-identifies data such as PII and credentials. It does not detect injection attempts or hateful content, so both red-team failures would remain.

choices.text: A detailed system instruction telling the model to refuse manipulation attempts and never produce hateful language, versioned in Git
choices.rationale: The instruction lives in the same context the attacker is manipulating, is configured per application rather than as central policy, and gives no independent screening of prompts or responses.

explanation: Content-level AI threats need a content-aware screen on both the input and output paths. Network and data-loss controls address different risks.

prompt: Cymbal's virtual shopping agent on Conversational Agents (Dialogflow CX) sometimes collects card details and delivery addresses, and the conversations flow into Cloud Logging and conversation history. Compliance requires that card numbers and personal data are redacted before they are written to logs, that Cymbal's own team decides what counts as sensitive, and that stored conversation data is kept for at most 90 days. Which two actions meet these requirements? Choose two.

choices.text: Create Sensitive Data Protection templates for card and personal infoTypes, grant the Dialogflow service identity access, and attach them in the agent's security settings.
choices.rationale: Security settings apply Sensitive Data Protection templates between Dialogflow CX and Cloud Logging, so data is redacted before publication. Cymbal defines the infoTypes, and the service identity needs template reader access.

choices.text: Rely on the default inspect template in the security settings, which already detects the common sensitive types without any configuration work.
choices.rationale: The default template enables only some infoType detectors and can be unreliable. Google recommends creating your own template so that Cymbal controls what counts as sensitive.

choices.text: Set a 90-day retention window in the same security settings, which is below the default 365-day limit, so persisted conversation data is purged on schedule.
choices.rationale: Retention is configured in security settings and must be lower than the default 365-day TTL. A 90-day window satisfies the maximum storage period for the persisted conversation data.

choices.text: Send logs to BigQuery through a log sink and run a nightly Sensitive Data Protection job that redacts the exported tables for analysts, auditors and reporting.
choices.rationale: Redacting downstream leaves raw card numbers in the original log entries and in the interval before the job runs. Redaction must happen at the source, before data reaches Cloud Logging.

choices.text: Mark only the card number parameter with Redact in logs and treat the other parts of each conversation as non-sensitive, since delivery data is public.
choices.rationale: Parameter redaction covers only the parameters flagged and nothing else. Delivery addresses and personal details elsewhere in the conversation would reach the logs unredacted.

explanation: Redaction and retention are both configured in the agent's security settings. Use your own Sensitive Data Protection templates rather than the default, and set the retention window explicitly.

prompt: EHR Healthcare manages employees and contractors in on-premises Microsoft Active Directory, with AD FS already deployed as the identity provider. The security team wants these users to sign in to the Google Cloud console and the gcloud CLI with their AD credentials and to receive access through AD group membership. They do not want to create, or keep synchronized, a second set of user accounts in Google. What should the architect set up?

choices.text: Cloud Identity with Google Cloud Directory Sync copying AD users and groups into Google accounts, plus SAML single sign-on to AD FS
choices.rationale: This is the classic federation pattern and it works, but it provisions and maintains a Google-managed identity for every user, which is exactly the second set of accounts the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Workforce Identity Federation, with a workforce identity pool whose provider trusts AD FS and IAM roles granted to mapped AD groups on folders
choices.rationale: Workforce Identity Federation is sync-less: users authenticate at the external identity provider, AD FS is a supported one, and attribute mapping exposes group membership to IAM allow policies, so no Google-managed user accounts are created.

choices.text: Workload Identity Federation, with a workload identity pool and provider for AD FS so that each employee signs in as a federated principal
choices.rationale: Workload Identity Federation lets non-human workloads, such as pipelines running elsewhere, call Google Cloud APIs. Employee sign-in is the job of Workforce Identity Federation. The names are similar but the use cases differ.

choices.text: Managed Service for Microsoft Active Directory with a forest trust to the on-premises domain, used as the identity store for Google Cloud
choices.rationale: Managed Microsoft AD runs domain controllers for AD-aware workloads on Google Cloud. IAM still authenticates people with Google identities, so a forest trust does not give AD users console or gcloud access.

explanation: When the existing identity provider must stay the single source of truth and no Google-side accounts are wanted, Workforce Identity Federation replaces directory synchronization. Directory sync with Cloud Identity remains valid when Google identities are acceptable.

prompt: EHR Healthcare loads insurer claim files into BigQuery every night. Analysts must count claims per patient and join each night's load to clinical tables on the patient ID, but must never see real identifiers. Compliance also requires that only a privileged backend service, acting on a legal request, can map a token back to the patient. The team will de-identify the patient ID column with Sensitive Data Protection. Which transformation meets all of these requirements?

choices.text: Cryptographic hashing with HMAC-SHA-256 and a Cloud KMS-wrapped key, applied to the patient ID column in each nightly load
choices.rationale: Keyed hashing is consistent across loads, so it supports the joins. It is one-way, so the privileged service could never recover the patient for the legal request.

choices.text: Deterministic encryption with AES-SIV, using one Cloud KMS-wrapped key that every nightly load shares
choices.rationale: The same key and input always give the same token, so joins and per-patient counts work across loads and tables. Whoever holds access to the KMS key can reverse tokens, and that access can be limited to the privileged service.

choices.text: Tokenization with a transient key that Sensitive Data Protection generates and discards for each de-identification request
choices.rationale: A transient key keeps tokens consistent only within one API request, so each night's tokens differ and cannot be joined. Because the key is discarded, re-identification is impossible too.

choices.text: Character masking that replaces all but the last four characters of each patient ID with an asterisk
choices.rationale: Masking does not create a token: different patients share the same last four characters, so counts and joins merge people, and the original ID cannot be recovered from what remains.

explanation: Pick the pseudonymization method from two properties: referential integrity (same input, same token) and reversibility. Deterministic encryption and format-preserving encryption give both, hashing gives only the first, and a transient key gives neither across requests.

prompt: KnightMotives Automotive plans to analyse European drivers' telemetry in BigQuery and to share a subset with commercial partners. EU counsel sets two requirements. First, a preventive control so that no team can create new datasets or buckets for this data outside the EU. Second, direct identifiers such as driver name and vehicle identification number must be pseudonymized before partners can query the shared tables. Which two actions together meet both requirements? Choose two.

choices.text: Apply the resource locations organization policy constraint with the in:eu-locations value group to the folder holding the telemetry projects
choices.rationale: The gcp.resourceLocations constraint stops supported services, including BigQuery and Cloud Storage, from creating new resources outside the allowed locations, which makes it a preventive control. It is not applied retroactively to resources that already exist.

choices.text: Run Sensitive Data Protection de-identification on the identifier columns with tokenization or redaction before publishing the shared tables
choices.rationale: De-identification transforms the sensitive values themselves, for example by redaction, masking or tokenization, so partners never see clear identifiers. Inspection alone would only report where identifiers are and would leave the data unchanged.

choices.text: Put the telemetry projects inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter so that the data cannot be copied to projects or buckets outside the perimeter
choices.rationale: A perimeter limits access paths and exfiltration between projects. It does not restrict the location where a dataset is created, and it does not change identifier values in the tables that partners can query.

choices.text: Create log-based alerts for dataset creation outside the EU and have an engineer delete each such dataset after it is flagged
choices.rationale: This control is detective rather than preventive. The out-of-region dataset already exists, and may already hold data, before anyone reacts, but the requirement is to stop its creation in the first place.

choices.text: Encrypt every dataset with Cloud KMS keys located in an EU region, so that the data stays in Europe and identifiers are unreadable to partners
choices.rationale: A key's location does not decide where a dataset can be created. Encryption at rest with CMEK is also transparent to authorized readers, so partners with access would still query the identifiers in clear text.

explanation: Meet a residency requirement with a preventive location constraint, and meet a pseudonymization requirement by transforming the data; access perimeters and key location address neither.

prompt: Altostrat Media's moderation service on Cloud Run asks a Gemini model on the Agent Platform to judge uploaded videos, passing Cloud Storage URIs and returning a verdict with reasoning. Auditors now require that, for any decision in the past 12 months, Altostrat can show which service identity called the model, the prompt, and the reasoning the model returned. The record must not depend on the moderation code itself. The exhibit shows the current state. What should the architect do?

exhibit.label: Current logging state
exhibit.content:
Control                                            | State
Admin Activity audit logs (Agent Platform API)     | On (default)
Data Access audit logs (Agent Platform API)        | Not enabled
Request-response logging for the Gemini model      | Off
Cloud Run application logs                         | Request ID and final verdict only

choices.text: Keep the current setup, since the Admin Activity audit logs that are already on record each model call along with its caller
choices.rationale: Admin Activity logs record API calls that modify the configuration or metadata of resources. Inference calls that read or process user data fall under Data Access logs, which the exhibit shows are not enabled.

choices.text: Enable Data Access audit logs for the Agent Platform API and log all Gemini requests and responses to BigQuery, kept 12 months
choices.rationale: Data Access logs are off by default and show who made calls. Request-response logging writes the request and response payloads for Gemini models to BigQuery at a chosen sampling rate, so a rate of 1 captures every decision, independent of app code.

choices.text: Have the Cloud Run service write each prompt and model reply to its application logs and extend log bucket retention to 12 months
choices.rationale: This record is produced by the very code under audit, so a bug or code change can silently drop or alter entries. It also does not capture the platform-level caller identity of the model request.

choices.text: Replace Gemini with a custom classifier and turn on Vertex Explainable AI feature attributions to explain each moderation verdict
choices.rationale: Feature attributions cover AutoML and custom-trained models, not Gemini calls, and the service is deprecated: access ends on or after March 16, 2027. A new model build also is not needed to log existing calls.

explanation: Auditable AI needs platform-level records of who called the model and what was sent and returned. Audit logs cover the caller, while request-response logging captures the payloads. At the time of verification, request-response logging was a Pre-GA feature and has a 10 MB row limit in BigQuery, so confirm its release stage against your compliance policy.

prompt: Altostrat Media employees sign in with Google Identity. Freelance editors at partner studios must open the Google Cloud console to review rough cuts and download files from one Cloud Storage review bucket. The studios authenticate with their own corporate OpenID Connect identity provider, and Altostrat does not want to create or administer Google accounts for people it does not employ. When a freelancer is removed at the studio, Altostrat should not need to take any action. What should the architect set up?

choices.text: Workforce Identity Federation with a pool that trusts the studio's OIDC provider, granting the bucket role to the studio's mapped group
choices.rationale: Workforce Identity Federation accepts any OIDC or SAML 2.0 provider without requiring Google accounts. Users reach the console through federated sign-in, and roles go to a principal set for a mapped group, so removal at the studio ends access.

choices.text: Cloud Identity accounts for each freelancer, with the studio's user directory synchronized by Google Cloud Directory Sync
choices.rationale: This creates the Google-managed accounts Altostrat wants to avoid, makes Altostrat administer them, and removal at the studio would not propagate until the synchronization runs and the account is suspended.

choices.text: Workload Identity Federation with a workload identity pool for the studio's provider, so each freelancer signs in as a federated principal
choices.rationale: Workload Identity Federation is for applications and pipelines outside Google Cloud calling APIs. Human sign-in to the console is the purpose of Workforce Identity Federation, though the names are easy to confuse.

choices.text: One service account per studio with a downloaded key stored in the studio's password manager and rotated when a freelancer leaves
choices.rationale: Long-lived keys are shared credentials that give no per-person identity or audit trail, require Altostrat to act on every departure, and do not provide console sign-in through the studio's identity provider.

explanation: For external people who already have an identity provider, federate that provider with Workforce Identity Federation instead of creating Google accounts, and grant roles to mapped groups so the provider stays the source of truth. Employees on Google Identity are unaffected.

prompt: EHR Healthcare's staff are managed in on-premises Microsoft Active Directory with AD FS deployed. Analysts also need Google identities, because IAM roles are granted to Google Groups and reports are shared through Google accounts. Security requires that Active Directory remain the only system that stores passwords and enforces MFA, that AD groups drive group membership in Google, and that joiners and leavers flow through without manual admin-console work. Choose two actions.

choices.text: Run Google Cloud Directory Sync on a schedule, using LDAP queries to provision AD users and groups into Cloud Identity one way
choices.rationale: Directory Sync reads the directory over LDAP and uses the Directory API to add, modify or delete users and groups on a schedule. Changes flow from Active Directory to Cloud Identity, which covers the joiner and leaver requirement.

choices.text: Configure SAML single sign-on in Cloud Identity with AD FS, so that AD authenticates users and keeps enforcing its password and MFA policy
choices.rationale: With SAML SSO, Cloud Identity delegates authentication to AD FS, so credentials and MFA stay in Active Directory. SSO handles sign-in only and needs the accounts to exist already, which is why it pairs with provisioning.

choices.text: Enable two-way synchronization in Google Cloud Directory Sync so that group edits made in Cloud Identity are written back to AD
choices.rationale: Provisioning is one way only. Changes in Active Directory replicate to Cloud Identity but not the other way around, and writing back would also break the rule that AD is the source of truth for groups.

choices.text: Configure SAML single sign-on alone and let each user's first successful sign-in create the Cloud Identity account and its group memberships
choices.rationale: SSO does not provision anything: a sign-on succeeds only if the user was provisioned beforehand. Without a directory sync there is no account to sign in to and no AD-driven group membership.

choices.text: Have each user choose a separate Google password at onboarding and enforce MFA in Cloud Identity, leaving AD for on-premises systems only
choices.rationale: This creates a second credential store with its own MFA policy, which is the opposite of keeping Active Directory as the only place that holds passwords and enforces MFA. Leavers would also keep working Google passwords.

explanation: Federating Cloud Identity with Active Directory takes two cooperating parts: scheduled one-way provisioning of users and groups, and SAML single sign-on that sends authentication back to AD FS. Neither part works well without the other. When no Google-side accounts are wanted at all, Workforce Identity Federation is the alternative.

prompt: KnightMotives suffered another breach: an attacker with a stolen service account key read telemetry exports from a Cloud Storage bucket. The exhibit summarizes what investigators found. Leadership wants the organization to be ready for the next incident, so that investigators can tell which principal read which objects, and so that this evidence survives even if a project owner is compromised. Which two actions together meet the goal? Choose two.

exhibit.label: Investigation notes for the affected project
exhibit.content:
Admin Activity audit log : 14 entries, including storage.setIamPermissions on the telemetry bucket
Storage Data Access audit log: no entries (no audit configuration set for Cloud Storage)
Log storage                  : _Default log bucket in the same project, default retention, editable by project owners
Conclusion                   : cannot establish which objects were read, or by whom

choices.text: Enable DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE audit logs for Cloud Storage in the organization-level audit configuration, so existing and new projects inherit them
choices.rationale: Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage are off by default, and they are the entries that record object reads. Configured at the organization, they apply to all current and future projects and child projects cannot turn them off.

choices.text: Route audit logs from the whole organization through an aggregated sink into a security-project log bucket with a locked retention policy
choices.rationale: An aggregated sink copies the entries out of every project into a separate project that workload owners do not control. A locked bucket retention policy is irreversible, so evidence cannot be shortened or the bucket removed before entries meet it.

choices.text: Rely on the Admin Activity audit logs that are always written, because they record which principals read the objects as well as who changed permissions
choices.rationale: Admin Activity logs cover calls that modify configuration or metadata, such as changing bucket permissions. Reads of user-provided data are recorded only in Data Access logs, which is why the exhibit shows nothing about object reads.

choices.text: Raise the retention of the _Default log bucket in every project to several years, so that read activity is kept long enough for any later investigation
choices.rationale: Longer retention only keeps entries that were written, and the read entries never existed. Project owners can also change the retention of these buckets, so the evidence stays within reach of a compromised owner.

choices.text: Enable Data Access audit logs only in the breached project, then extend the same configuration to the other projects after a later review
choices.rationale: Logs for the breached project would help only with that incident. Every other project and each new one stays blind to object reads until someone reconfigures it, whereas an organization-level setting closes the gap at once.

explanation: Forensic readiness needs two things: the missing Data Access entries must be generated everywhere, and they must be copied to storage that a compromised project owner cannot alter.

prompt: After repeated breaches, KnightMotives is rolling out mandatory security awareness training. The security lead also wants a technical control that still protects the organization when a person is fooled by a convincing phishing page. Employees sign in through SSO with MFA enforced at the corporate identity provider. A phished Cloud Identity super admin credential is rated the highest-impact scenario. Which control best addresses it?

choices.text: Enforce 2-Step Verification with security keys on super admin accounts in Cloud Identity itself, where they authenticate directly
choices.rationale: Super admins bypass the organization's SSO settings, so their protection must be configured in Cloud Identity. Security keys are phishing-resistant: a fake page cannot relay them, which is why the foundations guidance recommends them for super admins.

choices.text: Rely on the MFA already enforced at the corporate identity provider, since every sign-in to Cloud Identity is redirected there for verification first
choices.rationale: Super admin accounts are deliberately excluded from SSO so that they can still reach the console if SSO is misconfigured or down. Their sign-in never passes through the provider's MFA, so that control does not protect them.

choices.text: Enforce 2-Step Verification with codes sent by SMS for the super admin accounts, since a one-time code defeats a stolen password
choices.rationale: A one-time code defeats a password reused elsewhere but not a live phishing page, which can ask for the code and replay it at once. Only phishing-resistant factors such as security keys check where the sign-in happens.

choices.text: Require super admins to use longer passphrases that are rotated every month, and report the training completion rate to the board
choices.rationale: A phished credential is typed into the attacker's page by the user, so length and rotation add no protection against it. Rotation adds nothing when the attacker uses the credential immediately.

explanation: Super admin accounts sit outside SSO, so their phishing protection is a security key configured in Cloud Identity. Training lowers the odds of being fooled and a phishing-resistant factor limits the damage when it still happens.

prompt: Altostrat Media has retired the public bastion host and removed external IPs from the VMs that run its legacy ingest and archive tooling. Developers must still reach SSH and an internal admin console on those VMs, with access decided per user. After the cutover, tunneled sessions cannot connect. Using the exhibit, which change completes an IAP-based design without leaving the ports reachable from the internet?

exhibit.label: Network and IAM state for project altostrat-ingest
exhibit.content:
firewall_rules:           # network: ingest-vpc
  - name: allow-ssh-from-bastion
    direction: INGRESS
    priority: 1000
    source_ranges: [198.51.100.7/32]   # retired bastion public IP
    allowed: [tcp:22]
    target_tags: [ingest-vm]
  - name: allow-internal
    direction: INGRESS
    priority: 65534
    source_ranges: [10.20.0.0/16]
    allowed: [all]
iam_bindings:
  - group:ingest-devs@altostrat.example: roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor
  - group:ingest-devs@altostrat.example: roles/compute.osLogin
vm:
  name: ingest-vm-01
  tags: [ingest-vm]
  external_ip: none
  metadata: {enable-oslogin: "TRUE"}
  admin_console_port: 8443

choices.text: Add an ingress allow rule for tcp:22 and tcp:8443 from 35.235.240.0/20 to the ingest-vm tag, and delete the stale bastion rule.
choices.rationale: IAP TCP forwarding reaches the VM from Google's 35.235.240.0/20 range, so the VPC needs an ingress rule for that range on each forwarded port. The only SSH rule trusts the retired bastion's address, and nothing admits the console port. Deleting the stale rule removes a dead trust relationship.

choices.text: Set the bastion rule's source range to 0.0.0.0/0 and add tcp:8443, because tunneled traffic can arrive from any address.
choices.rationale: IAP traffic arrives from one documented range, not from any address. Opening the ports to every source would make them reachable from the internet and defeat per-user, identity-aware access.

choices.text: Create a Cloud NAT gateway on ingest-vpc so that the IAP tunnel can reach the VMs' internal addresses through the new path.
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT handles outbound connections for VMs that lack external IPs. It does not carry inbound IAP connections, so the firewall would still drop the tunnel traffic.

choices.text: Grant the developer group roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 on the project, since the tunnel and OS Login roles alone are not enough.
choices.rationale: The exhibit already grants the tunnel role and the OS Login role, which are what the IAP and SSH flow need. A broader administrator role adds privilege, and no IAM role can open a path that the firewall blocks.

prompt: Lumen Credit serves a custom-trained credit-risk model from Vertex AI online inference. Three internal applications call it, each in its own project and VPC network, and the network team will not create VPC peering connections for this. Security requires that requests reach the model over private IP addresses in each application's VPC, that only those three projects can send requests, and that the serving project stays inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter. Which endpoint design meets these requirements?

choices.text: A dedicated private endpoint on Private Service Connect, with the three projects in its allowlist and a forwarding rule in each VPC.
choices.rationale: Private Service Connect serves inference to multiple consumer projects and VPC networks without public IPs, public internet access, or peered ranges. The project allowlist limits who can send requests, and the private endpoint supports the perimeter.

choices.text: A private services access endpoint, with the serving project's network peered to Google's service network and the three VPCs routed to it.
choices.rationale: Private services access depends on VPC peering, which the network team has ruled out. It also binds all private endpoints in a project to a single network, so it fits several separate consumer VPCs poorly.

choices.text: A dedicated public endpoint, which Google recommends for serving, with only the three applications' service accounts granted invoker roles.
choices.rationale: Dedicated public endpoints isolate traffic from other users but remain public endpoints, so requests do not arrive over private addresses in each VPC. VPC Service Controls is not supported on them either.

choices.text: A shared public endpoint kept inside the perimeter, with ingress rules that admit only the three applications' projects and identities.
choices.rationale: A perimeter controls who may call the service, but it does not change the endpoint type. This remains a public endpoint, so the requirement to reach the model over private IP addresses in each VPC is not met.

prompt: Meridian Pay processes card payments on Google Cloud. Auditors require that the keys protecting its BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets be generated and used inside FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware. The security team wants Google to operate that hardware, with rotation and access handled through Cloud KMS, and sees no need to hold key material outside Google. Which key configuration should the architect choose?

choices.text: Cloud KMS keys at the software protection level as CMEK, because the cryptographic module behind them is FIPS validated.
choices.rationale: Software keys use a FIPS 140-3 Level 1 validated module. That suits workloads with no higher validation requirement, but it does not satisfy a Level 3 hardware mandate.

choices.text: Cloud EKM keys held in an external key manager and reached over a VPC network, for the strongest possible key custody.
choices.rationale: External keys are warranted when key material must live outside Google. Nothing here needs that, and it adds dependence on a partner system whose availability Google cannot control, at the highest cost.

choices.text: Cloud KMS keys at the HSM protection level, used as CMEK on BigQuery and Cloud Storage, with Google operating the HSMs.
choices.rationale: Cloud HSM generates and uses keys in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs that Google operates. Keys work with CMEK integrations and Cloud KMS rotation and IAM, which matches every stated requirement.

choices.text: Single-tenant Cloud HSM keys, with the security team creating and administering its own dedicated HSM instance for the keys.
choices.rationale: A single-tenant instance adds cryptographic isolation, but the customer must create and administer it. The team asked for Google to operate the hardware and has no isolation requirement, so this adds cost and effort without need.

prompt: BrightLeaf is launching a reading app for children aged 6 to 12, with learner profiles in Firestore and analytics in BigQuery. Its counsel asks the architect who owns and controls the children's data once it is on Google Cloud, and who is accountable for obtaining parental consent under COPPA. Which answer should the architect give, and what should the design include?

choices.text: BrightLeaf owns the data; Google processes it per the contract. Consent is BrightLeaf's duty, so build consent and deletion flows into the app.
choices.rationale: Google's commitments are that customer data is the customer's and is processed only per the agreement. Its privacy mapping lists minors' consent as a customer responsibility based on its own business operations, so the app must handle consent and deletion.

choices.text: Google becomes controller of the stored profiles, so its published compliance reports already cover consent and the app needs no consent flow.
choices.rationale: Under the Cloud Data Processing Addendum Google is a processor and the customer is a controller or processor. Compliance reports describe Google's controls and do not transfer the customer's consent duties.

choices.text: Google owns the data once uploaded, so encrypt it with CMEK to stop Google from processing the profiles, and treat that as the COPPA control.
choices.rationale: Ownership never passes to Google, so the premise is wrong. CMEK protects data at rest and does not capture parental consent, which COPPA requires from the operator of the service.

choices.text: Keep all children's data in a US region, because COPPA is satisfied by storing the data in the country where the law was enacted.
choices.rationale: COPPA concerns consent for collecting children's personal information, not where the data sits. Region choice helps with residency rules, but it creates no consent and shifts no responsibility.

prompt: Northwind Freight lets each product team ship its own generative AI features. An internal review found one team screening prompts with a home-grown regex filter, another screening only model responses, and a third doing no screening at all. The security lead wants to apply the Secure AI Framework element "harmonize platform-level controls to ensure consistent security across the organization" to prompt and response screening. Teams may tighten the baseline for their own apps but must never fall below it. Which approach on Google Cloud fits?

choices.text: Set organization-level Model Armor floor settings with minimum prompt-injection, jailbreak and safety thresholds that no template can undercut.
choices.rationale: Floor settings define minimum filter requirements across the resource hierarchy, and Model Armor rejects any template that is less strict than the floor. That gives one enforced baseline while still letting a team create a stricter template for its own app, which is the harmonize-platform-level-controls element in practice.

choices.text: Publish an approved internal filtering library, require every team to adopt it, and verify that adoption during each product launch review.
choices.rationale: Shared code is consistency by convention. Nothing stops a team from skipping the library, calling a model directly or loosening its thresholds after launch, so the baseline is not enforced at the platform level. The home-grown regex filter in the stem is the same pattern, just centralised.

choices.text: Have each team create its own Model Armor template for its app, and let the security team review the chosen thresholds at each launch.
choices.rationale: Templates alone give every team a capable filter but no minimum. Without a floor setting, each team can pick permissive thresholds and the launch review is the only gate. Per-team templates are the right tool for tightening above a baseline, not for creating one.

choices.text: Turn on Data Access audit logs for every model endpoint, and have the security team review those logs for unscreened calls every week.
choices.rationale: Monitoring model inputs and outputs belongs to a different SAIF element, extending detection and response to AI. Audit logs report after the fact that screening was missing, but they do not prevent a team from shipping a weaker control, which is what the harmonizing element asks for.

explanation: SAIF's six elements are not a checklist to apply in order. Harmonizing platform-level controls means moving a control from each application into the platform, and for LLM screening on Google Cloud that is a floor setting that every Model Armor template must meet. Detection and response (monitoring, logging) is a separate element that complements it. One caveat: floor settings do not check templates for Sensitive Data Protection conformance.

prompt: Tallis Insurance runs dozens of product teams under one production folder. Today every customer-managed encryption key is requested through a ticket queue, and teams wait days to create a CMEK-protected bucket or disk. Requirements: developers must not be able to view or manage keys; keys must live in a project that only the security team administers; those administrators must not gain encrypt or decrypt access to data; HSM-backed keys with a yearly rotation are acceptable. One legacy analytics workload must run in a location where Cloud HSM is unavailable. Which design meets every requirement?

choices.text: Enable Cloud KMS Autokey on the production folder with dedicated-project key storage, and create a manual CMEK for the one legacy workload.
choices.rationale: Developers request a key during resource creation, and Autokey's service agent creates and binds it. Developers can only request creation, not view or manage keys. Keys land in the security team's key project, and key administrators get no encrypt or decrypt permissions. Autokey does not create keys where Cloud HSM is unavailable, so that workload needs a manual CMEK.

choices.text: Enable Autokey in same-project mode across the folder and give each team Cloud KMS Admin on its own project to tune rotation.
choices.rationale: Same-project storage creates keys inside the resource projects, so the keys no longer live in a security-only project. Giving developers Cloud KMS Admin lets them manage the keys, which breaks the requirement that developers neither view nor manage keys.

choices.text: Enable Autokey on the folder with dedicated-project storage for all workloads and rely on it to fall back to a software key where Cloud HSM is unavailable.
choices.rationale: Autokey creates HSM-protected keys in the same location as the resource and does not substitute software keys. Where Cloud HSM is not supported, the key cannot be created, so the legacy workload would be blocked rather than quietly covered by a weaker key.

choices.text: Keep manual CMEK, pre-create a key ring per team in the central key project, and bind each service agent to its team's key as requests arrive.
choices.rationale: Manual CMEK in a central project can satisfy the separation requirements, and it also covers the legacy location. It keeps the security team in the request path for every new resource, though, so the ticket-queue delay the stem wants to eliminate remains.

explanation: Autokey fits when many teams need compliant CMEK on demand: administrators enable it on a folder, keys use HSM protection and AES-256 GCM with a one-year default rotation, and the service agent handles key creation and IAM bindings. Manual CMEK remains the answer for locations without Cloud HSM and for anything outside Autokey's fixed key attributes.

prompt: Kestrel Fitness, an EU habit-tracking app, receives a verified erasure request from a former user. Her data sits in the production Cloud SQL database, a nightly BigQuery analytics copy, CSV exports in a Cloud Storage bucket used by the coaching team, and Cloud SQL automated backups kept for 30 days. Which plan fulfils the request?

choices.text: Delete or anonymize her data in Cloud SQL, BigQuery and the exports now, let backups age out within their retention window, and re-apply it after restores.
choices.rationale: Erasure reaches every store holding the person's data, including analytics copies and exports. Backups are handled by a bounded retention window plus re-applying deletions on restore, so she does not reappear.

choices.text: Delete her row in Cloud SQL, since the BigQuery tables and CSV exports are only derived copies of it and the database remains the system of record for her data.
choices.rationale: Derived copies are not exempt. Analytics tables and exports still hold her personal data and fall inside the request.

choices.text: Enable CMEK on every store and rotate the key regularly, so that the copies she appears in can no longer be read by the analytics or coaching teams.
choices.rationale: Encryption is not deletion. CMEK and rotation leave the data in place, and older key versions stay usable, so authorized principals can still read her records.

choices.text: Limit the BigQuery tables, exports and backups to a small admin group with IAM, and log every access to her records so that each one can be reviewed later.
choices.rationale: Access control is not erasure. Restricting and logging access leaves the data stored, so the duty to delete is still unmet.

explanation: Erasure means deletion or irreversible anonymization everywhere the person's data lives. Security controls limit who can read data; they do not remove it.

prompt: HaulPath, a freight-booking app, keeps customer-support chat transcripts containing personal data in a Cloud Storage bucket. The transcripts are only needed for 90 days of dispute handling, yet nothing removes them today. Which configuration implements storage limitation for this data?

choices.text: An Object Lifecycle Management rule on the bucket with a Delete action that applies when an object reaches an age of 90 days.
choices.rationale: Lifecycle Delete rules remove objects automatically when their conditions are met, which turns the 90-day purpose-based retention period into automated deletion.

choices.text: A retention policy of 90 days on the bucket, so that each transcript is removed automatically once it reaches that age.
choices.rationale: A retention policy only blocks deletion and replacement until the age is reached. Nothing deletes the object afterwards, so transcripts would stay indefinitely.

choices.text: A lifecycle rule that moves transcripts to the Coldline storage class after 90 days, keeping them cheaply available for later disputes.
choices.rationale: Changing the storage class lowers cost but keeps the data. Cheaper storage is still indefinite retention, which is the opposite of storage limitation.

choices.text: Soft delete turned off on the bucket, so that any transcript staff delete is gone immediately instead of being recoverable for a while.
choices.rationale: Soft delete only governs how long already-deleted objects stay recoverable. Disabling it triggers no scheduled deletion of transcripts.

explanation: Storage limitation needs a retention period tied to purpose plus automated deletion. A retention policy and lifecycle Delete rule are different tools: one blocks early deletion, the other performs the deletion.

prompt: Ledgerly, a payments company, receives a verified erasure request. Local financial regulation obliges it to keep transaction records for seven years, and they sit in a Cloud Storage bucket with a locked seven-year retention policy. The customer's marketing profile, contact preferences and analytics events, which carry no retention duty, live in Firestore and BigQuery. How should Ledgerly respond?

choices.text: Erase the profile, preference and analytics data now, keep the regulated transactions restricted to their legal purpose, and delete them when the period ends.
choices.rationale: Erasure has an exception for legal obligations. Data without a retention duty is erased, the regulated records are kept and restricted, and they are deleted automatically when the duty ends. Counsel confirms the classification.

choices.text: Delete everything immediately, including the transaction records, because the right to erasure overrides every other legal obligation and the locked policy can be lifted first.
choices.rationale: Erasure is not absolute, and a locked retention policy cannot be removed or shortened, so it would block the deletion anyway. Deleting regulated records would also breach the retention duty.

choices.text: Decline the whole request, because a customer with records under a retention duty loses the right to erasure for all of the personal data held about them.
choices.rationale: The exception covers only data needed for the legal obligation. Over-applying it to the profile and analytics data leaves erasable data in place.

choices.text: Destroy the Cloud KMS key protecting the transaction bucket, which satisfies erasure while the locked policy keeps the encrypted objects in place.
choices.rationale: Destroying the key makes the records unreadable, which defeats the duty to retain usable records, and it affects every object under that key. It also leaves the profile and analytics data untouched.
